topic: reading and writing files in Python

questions.question: What do the main Python file modes mean?
questions.title: Python File Modes: r, w, a, x, b, and +
questions.direct_answer: `r` reads, `w` replaces, `a` appends, `x` creates only a new file, `b` selects bytes, and `+` allows both reading and writing.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether mode flags are connected to creation, overwrite, and data representation.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Describing `w` as harmless writing without mentioning immediate truncation.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Choose the mode from the intended file lifecycle and state the destructive boundary.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: `r` is the default and fails when the path does not exist.
`w` creates a file or truncates an existing file immediately.
`a` creates if needed and writes at the end; `x` fails if the path exists.
`b` reads and writes `bytes`; text mode reads and writes `str`.
`+` adds updating, but the file position still controls where operations occur.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
The mode passed to `open()` defines whether a file can be read, replaced, appended to, or created exclusively. `r` is the default read mode and requires the file to exist. `w` opens for writing, creating the file when needed but truncating an existing file as soon as it is opened. `a` also creates when needed, but writes are placed at the end. `x` performs exclusive creation and raises `FileExistsError` rather than replacing an existing path.

Text mode is the default and returns `str`; adding `b` selects binary mode and returns `bytes`. The `+` flag creates an updating mode that supports both reads and writes, such as `r+` or `w+`. It does not remove the other mode's behaviour: `w+` still truncates, and switching between reads and writes requires attention to the current file position and buffering.

For example, replacing a generated report can use `w`, recording a new audit line can use `a`, and creating a lock-like marker without overwriting an existing one can use `x`. Images need `rb` or `wb`, while JSON and source files normally use text mode with an explicit encoding such as UTF-8.

The destructive boundary matters most: choose `w` only when replacing the old content is intentional. In normal code, combine the chosen mode with `with open(...)` so the handle is closed even if work fails.

sections.title: A mode combines access, creation, and representation
sections.content:
A file mode answers three separate questions. The first is access: read, write, append, or update. The second is creation behaviour: require an existing path, create if absent, replace existing content, or refuse to overwrite. The third is representation: translated text or exact bytes. Reading the flags through those three decisions makes combinations easier to understand.

Opening with `w` changes the file before the first call to `write`, so an exception after `open` may still leave an empty file. When safe replacement matters, applications often write to a temporary file and then replace the destination. Append mode is suitable for independent records, but it does not make a complete multi-process record protocol automatically safe.

Update modes share one stream position. A read moves that position forward; a later write starts at the resulting position unless append semantics apply. `seek()` and `tell()` make position explicit, but separate read and write phases are often simpler.

sections.title: Creation and overwrite behaviour
sections.content:
| Base mode | Must exist? | Creates missing file? | Existing content |
|---|---:|---:|---|
| `r` | Yes | No | Preserved |
| `w` | No | Yes | Truncated |
| `a` | No | Yes | Preserved; writes go to end |
| `x` | Must not exist | Yes | Never overwritten |

Add `b` for bytes and `+` for read-and-write access.

sections.title: Exercise safe creation, replacement, and append
sections.content:
```python
from pathlib import Path
from tempfile import TemporaryDirectory

with TemporaryDirectory() as folder:
    path = Path(folder) / "events.txt"

    with path.open("x", encoding="utf-8") as handle:
        handle.write("created\n")

    with path.open("a", encoding="utf-8") as handle:
        handle.write("second\n")

    with path.open("r", encoding="utf-8") as handle:
        assert handle.read() == "created\nsecond\n"
```

followup_questions: Why can opening with `w` lose data before `write()` is called?
What is the difference between `a` and `x`?
What does `+` change, and what does it leave unchanged?

questions.question: What is the difference between read(), readline(), readlines(), and file iteration?
questions.title: Python File Reading Methods
questions.direct_answer: `read()` returns all or a requested chunk, `readline()` returns one line, `readlines()` builds a list, and iteration yields lines lazily.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether file reads are understood as stream operations with memory consequences.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Assuming every read starts from the beginning or that iteration first builds a list.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Choose the result shape deliberately and account for the current stream position.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: `read()` without a size loads the remaining content into one value.
`read(size)` reads up to a requested number of characters or bytes.
`readline()` returns one line and normally keeps its line ending.
`readlines()` returns a list of all remaining lines.
Iterating over the file processes one line at a time and is usually best for large text files.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
Python file objects support several reading shapes. `read()` returns the remaining content as one string in text mode or one bytes object in binary mode; an optional size limits the requested chunk. `readline()` returns a single line, including its newline when present. `readlines()` consumes the remaining stream and returns a list of lines. Direct iteration, `for line in file`, yields lines one by one.

For example, a small configuration file can be loaded with `read()` because its size is known and limited. A multi-gigabyte log should normally be iterated so only a small part is held at once. `readlines()` is convenient only when a real list is needed and the input comfortably fits in memory. `readline()` is useful for protocols or formats where the next line has a particular meaning.

Every operation advances the stream position. Calling `read()` twice does not restart the file; the second call begins where the first stopped and may return an empty value at end-of-file. `seek()` can reposition seekable files, but a single forward pass is simpler when possible. The choice is therefore based on required shape and memory use, not just syntax.

sections.title: A file object is a stateful stream
sections.content:
A stream has a current position. Each successful read consumes data and moves that position. End-of-file is represented by an empty string in text mode or empty bytes in binary mode, not by an exception. That state explains many beginner surprises after one method has already consumed the input.

Iteration uses the file object's iterator protocol and preserves line boundaries without building a list first. It is both readable and memory-friendly for line-oriented data. Chunked `read(size)` is more suitable when records are not line-based or when bytes are being copied.

Line methods usually retain the newline, so use `rstrip("\n")` when only that delimiter should be removed. Plain `strip()` also removes leading and trailing spaces and may accidentally alter meaningful data.

sections.title: Choose by result shape and memory
sections.content:
| Operation | Returns | Memory shape | Useful for |
|---|---|---|---|
| `read()` | One `str` or `bytes` value | Entire remainder | Small, bounded input |
| `read(size)` | One limited chunk | Bounded chunk | Copying or non-line data |
| `readline()` | One line | One line | Header or protocol step |
| `readlines()` | List of remaining lines | Entire remainder plus list | Small input needing a list |
| `for line in file` | Lines over time | One line at a time | Large line-oriented input |

sections.title: See how reads advance the position
sections.content:
```python
from io import StringIO

stream = StringIO("alpha\nbeta\ngamma\n")
assert stream.readline() == "alpha\n"
assert stream.read(4) == "beta"
assert stream.tell() > 0
assert stream.readlines() == ["\n", "gamma\n"]
assert stream.read() == ""

stream.seek(0)
assert [line.rstrip("\n") for line in stream] == ["alpha", "beta", "gamma"]
```

followup_questions: Why can `readlines()` be expensive for a large file?
What does a read return at end-of-file?
Why might `rstrip("\n")` be safer than `strip()` for line data?

questions.question: What is the difference between text and binary file I/O in Python?
questions.title: Text vs Binary File I/O in Python
questions.direct_answer: Text mode converts file bytes to `str` using an encoding and may translate newlines; binary mode returns exact `bytes` without either conversion.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether text conversion is distinguished from exact byte I/O.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Calling a binary format text or relying on an environment-specific default encoding.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Treat encoding as part of the external data contract and convert once at the boundary.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: Text mode reads and writes `str`; binary mode reads and writes bytes-like values.
Text mode decodes and encodes through the selected character encoding.
Specify `encoding="utf-8"` for known UTF-8 text instead of relying on the platform default.
Binary mode performs no encoding or newline translation.
Use text mode for human text and binary mode for images, archives, and protocol bytes.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
Text and binary I/O expose different data contracts. A text stream returns `str` and accepts `str` for writing. Python decodes the file's bytes when reading and encodes characters when writing, using the selected encoding. It may also translate platform line endings. A binary stream returns `bytes`, accepts bytes-like data, and performs neither character conversion nor newline translation.

For example, a UTF-8 CSV file should normally be opened in text mode with `encoding="utf-8"`, because the program wants characters and lines. A PNG must be opened with `rb` or `wb`, because its bytes are not text and must remain exact. Passing `encoding` in binary mode is invalid, and writing a `str` to a binary stream, or `bytes` to a text stream, raises `TypeError`.

The encoding is part of the data format, not a cosmetic option. The default text encoding can depend on the environment, so a file that works on one machine may fail or decode differently on another. New applications should specify the known encoding at the boundary. Error policies such as ignoring undecodable bytes can lose information, so strict decoding is a safer default unless the product has an explicit recovery rule.

In short, use text mode when bytes represent characters under a known encoding, and binary mode when byte-for-byte identity matters.

sections.title: Text I/O is a conversion layer over bytes
sections.content:
Storage ultimately contains bytes. A text wrapper sits above a binary buffer and applies a codec in both directions. Decoding maps byte sequences to Unicode code points; encoding maps Python characters back to bytes. If the chosen codec does not match the file, decoding can fail or produce incorrect characters.

Newline handling is another text-layer service. On reading, universal newline processing can present different platform endings as `\n`. On writing, text mode may map `\n` to the platform convention. This convenience is correct for text but would change a binary format.

A clean design performs conversion once at the system boundary. Internal business logic works with `str` for text or `bytes` for binary data, rather than repeatedly guessing encodings. If a protocol declares UTF-8, that declaration should appear explicitly in the open or decode call.

sections.title: The conversion boundary
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart LR
  F[Bytes in file] -->|binary mode| B[bytes in Python]
  F -->|decode with encoding| S[str in Python]
  S -->|encode with encoding| F
  B -->|binary write| F
```

sections.title: Round-trip the same text as characters and bytes
sections.content:
```python
from pathlib import Path
from tempfile import TemporaryDirectory

with TemporaryDirectory() as folder:
    path = Path(folder) / "greeting.txt"
    with path.open("w", encoding="utf-8") as handle:
        handle.write("नमस्ते\n")

    with path.open("r", encoding="utf-8") as handle:
        assert handle.read() == "नमस्ते\n"

    with path.open("rb") as handle:
        raw = handle.read()
        assert isinstance(raw, bytes)
        assert raw.decode("utf-8") == "नमस्ते\n"
```

What types do text and binary streams accept?
